```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4)
has_pscl <- requireNamespace("pscl", quietly = TRUE)
```

Many count datasets have many zeros. That alone says little: a count
distribution with a small mean or a large variance produces many zeros by
itself. This vignette shows how to tell whether a model needs a separate
zero process, what zero-inflated and hurdle models assume, how flexCountReg
labels their components, and why a zero-heavy sample is not the same thing
as a zero-truncated sampling design.

```{r setup}
library(flexCountReg)
```

## Three ways to produce zeros

| Process | Zeros come from | Model in flexCountReg |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary count | the count distribution only | any family |
| Zero-inflated | a separate "always zero" group *and* the count distribution | `zero_formula`, `zero_type = "inflated"` |
| Hurdle | a binary process for zero vs positive; positive counts from a zero-truncated count distribution | `zero_formula`, `zero_type = "hurdle"` |

The component labels differ between the two zero models, and so do the
meanings of their coefficients:

| | Zero-inflated | Hurdle |
|---|---|---|
| `Zero:` coefficients model (logit) | $\pi$ = probability of a structural zero | $q$ = probability of a *positive* count |
| A positive `Zero:` coefficient means | more structural zeros | fewer zeros |
| $P(Y = 0)$ | $\pi + (1 - \pi) f(0)$ | $1 - q$ |
| `predict(type = "zero")` returns | $\pi$ | $P(Y = 0) = 1 - q$ |

These are the conventions of the pscl package (Zeileis et al., 2008).

## A simulation: what each model finds

Three datasets of 1,000 counts with the same covariate `x` are simulated: an
ordinary NB2 count, a zero-inflated NB2 count (25% structural zeros) and a
hurdle count. All three have many zeros:

```{r simulate}
set.seed(12)
n <- 1000
x <- rnorm(n)
mu <- exp(0.3 + 0.5 * x)
y_nb <- rnbinom(n, size = 1, mu = mu)
y_zi <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.25, 0, rnbinom(n, size = 1, mu = mu))
# hurdle: positive with probability 0.55, then a zero-truncated NB2 count
draw_pos <- function(m) { repeat { v <- rnbinom(1, size = 1, mu = m)
  if (v > 0) return(v) } }
y_h <- ifelse(runif(n) < 0.55, vapply(mu, draw_pos, 0), 0)
sims <- data.frame(x, y_nb, y_zi, y_h)
sapply(sims[-1], function(y) mean(y == 0))
```

For each dataset, fit NB2, a zero-inflated NB2 and a hurdle NB2 with a
constant zero model, and compare AIC:

```{r sim-fits}
fit_three <- function(resp) {
  f <- reformulate("x", resp)
  list(NB2 = countreg(f, data = sims, family = "NB2", method = "BFGS"),
       ZINB = suppressWarnings(
         countreg(f, data = sims, family = "NB2", zero_formula = ~ 1,
                  method = "BFGS")),
       hurdle = countreg(f, data = sims, family = "NB2", zero_formula = ~ 1,
                         zero_type = "hurdle", method = "BFGS"))
}
sim_fits <- lapply(c(ordinary = "y_nb", zero_inflated = "y_zi",
                     hurdle = "y_h"), fit_three)
aic <- t(sapply(sim_fits, function(m) sapply(m, AIC)))
round(aic, 1)
```

```{r sim-best, include = FALSE}
best <- colnames(aic)[apply(aic, 1, which.min)]
gap_zi <- aic["zero_inflated", "NB2"] - aic["zero_inflated", "ZINB"]
```

The lowest AIC in each row belongs to
`r paste(best, collapse = ", ")` (ordinary, zero-inflated and hurdle data
in turn). For the ordinary count, the estimated structural-zero
probability is small
(`r signif(plogis(coef(sim_fits$ordinary$ZINB)[["Zero:(Intercept)"]]), 2)`)
and the extra parameter only costs AIC. For the zero-inflated data, with
25% structural zeros and 1,000 rows, the zero-inflated model improves the
AIC of NB2 by only `r round(gap_zi, 1)`: an NB2 distribution with a larger
dispersion can reproduce much of the same zero share. Real zero processes
are rarely as clean as these, so expect small differences.

## Real data: articles by PhD biochemists

`pscl::bioChemists` (Long, 1990) records the number of articles `art`
published in the last three years of the PhD by 915 biochemists, with
gender `fem`, marital status `mar`, the number of children under six
`kid5`, the prestige of the PhD department `phd` and the number of articles
of the mentor `ment` (not of the student).

```{r biochem, eval = has_pscl}
e <- new.env()
utils::data("bioChemists", package = "pscl", envir = e)
b <- e$bioChemists
c(n = nrow(b), share_zero = mean(b$art == 0), mean = mean(b$art),
  variance = var(b$art))
```

```{r biochem-skip, echo = FALSE, results = "asis", eval = !has_pscl}
cat("*The pscl package is not installed, so this section is not run.*")
```

### Baselines: how many zeros does an ordinary model expect?

```{r baselines, eval = has_pscl}
f <- art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment
pois <- countreg(f, data = b, family = "POISSON", method = "BFGS")
nb2 <- countreg(f, data = b, family = "NB2", method = "BFGS")
zeros <- c(observed = mean(b$art == 0),
           poisson = mean(predict(pois, type = "prob", max_count = 0)[, 1]),
           nb2 = mean(predict(nb2, type = "prob", max_count = 0)[, 1]))
round(zeros, 3)
```

The Poisson model expects too few zeros, but the NB2 model, which allows
for overdispersion, already expects about as many zeros as observed. The
"excess" zeros relative to Poisson are explained by overdispersion; they do
not by themselves call for a separate zero process.

### Zero-inflated and hurdle models

```{r zero-models, eval = has_pscl}
zinb_const <- countreg(f, data = b, family = "NB2", zero_formula = ~ 1,
                       method = "BFGS")
zinb <- countreg(f, data = b, family = "NB2",
                 zero_formula = ~ ment + kid5, method = "BFGS")
hnb <- countreg(f, data = b, family = "NB2",
                zero_formula = ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment,
                zero_type = "hurdle", method = "BFGS")
```

With a constant zero model, the structural-zero probability is driven to the
boundary: the warning above says that its likelihood is flat, and its
standard error is `NA`:

```{r zinb-const, eval = has_pscl}
summary(zinb_const)$coefficients["Zero:(Intercept)", 1:2]
plogis(coef(zinb_const)[["Zero:(Intercept)"]])
```

With covariates, the zero model can describe *which* students have more
zeros. In the zero-inflated model a negative `Zero:ment` coefficient means
fewer structural zeros among students of productive mentors; in the hurdle
model the `Zero:` coefficients describe the probability of publishing at
least one article:

```{r zero-coefs, eval = has_pscl}
zc <- function(m) {
  co <- summary(m)$coefficients
  co[grep("^Zero:", rownames(co)), 1:2]
}
zc(zinb)
zc(hnb)
```

flexCountReg's likelihoods and zero-model coefficients agree with those of
pscl:

```{r pscl-check, eval = has_pscl}
z_ref <- pscl::zeroinfl(art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment | ment + kid5,
                        data = b, dist = "negbin")
h_ref <- pscl::hurdle(art ~ fem + mar + kid5 + phd + ment, data = b,
                      dist = "negbin")
c(zinb = as.numeric(logLik(zinb)), pscl_zinb = as.numeric(logLik(z_ref)),
  hurdle = as.numeric(logLik(hnb)), pscl_hurdle = as.numeric(logLik(h_ref)))
```

### Probability accounting

Each model's fitted probabilities can be compared with the observed
frequencies, count by count, on the same rows. The overall expected count
(including the zero component) is the mean prediction:

```{r accounting, eval = has_pscl}
models <- list(Poisson = pois, NB2 = nb2, ZINB = zinb, hurdle = hnb)
probs <- sapply(models, function(m)
  colMeans(predict(m, type = "prob", max_count = 5)))
acct <- rbind(round(cbind(observed = tabulate(b$art + 1, 6) / nrow(b),
                          probs), 3),
              mean_count = round(c(mean(b$art),
                                   sapply(models, function(m)
                                     mean(predict(m)))), 3))
acct
```

The mean predictions of all four models are close to the observed mean, so
the mean alone cannot separate them. The NB2, zero-inflated and hurdle
models reproduce the zeros and small counts about equally well; the Poisson
model does not.

```{r compare, eval = has_pscl}
data.frame(model = names(models),
           logLik = sapply(models, function(m) as.numeric(logLik(m))),
           AIC = sapply(models, AIC), row.names = NULL)
```

The zero-inflated and hurdle models with covariates have lower AIC than NB2.
That shows that the probability of a zero varies with the covariates in a
way that the NB2 mean model does not capture; it does not establish that
some students are "structural non-publishers". A large share of zeros, or a
better fit of a zero model, is evidence about the fit, not proof of a
particular mechanism.

### Which comparisons are valid

The NB2 model is the zero-inflated NB2 model with $\pi = 0$, which is on
the boundary of the parameter space (an intercept of $-\infty$ on the logit
scale), so the usual likelihood-ratio test does not apply and flexCountReg
does not report one. Compare such models with AIC or BIC on the same rows,
or on held-out data (`vignette("predictive-validation", package =
"flexCountReg")`). When a zero-model probability is estimated near 0 or 1,
its Wald standard errors are unreliable, as the `NA` above shows.

## A zero-truncated sample is a different problem

A hurdle model says that zeros happen and come from a separate process. A
*zero-truncated sampling design* says that zeros cannot be observed at all:
for example, counts of visits recorded only for people who visited at least
once. Having no zeros in the data, or few zeros by chance, is not the same
as truncation. Under truncation the likelihood of each observation is
$f(y) / (1 - f(0))$ for $y \ge 1$; this is the positive part of a hurdle
model, but fitting a hurdle model to truncated data (where no zeros exist
to estimate the binary part) is not a substitute. flexCountReg does not yet
provide a zero-truncated estimator.

## Reproducibility and next steps

The simulation uses `set.seed(12)`; the bioChemists data come from the pscl
package.

* `vignette("diagnosing-count-models", package = "flexCountReg")` shows
  calibration checks for zeros and large counts.
* `vignette("choosing-a-count-distribution", package = "flexCountReg")`
  compares observed and expected zeros on road-crash data.
